beats.script_body: Founded in 1804, the New-York Historical Society is the city's oldest museum, presenting a look back at the history of the United States through the lens of New York. Even the hyphen in its name is a history lesson: it follows a convention used until the 1840s. The renovated galleries draw on a collection of sixty thousand artifacts and works of art spanning four centuries.

beats.script_body: When the Dakota was completed in 1884, designed by Henry J. Hardenbergh, the Upper West Side was so desolate that the building was named after the remote Dakota Territory. But the distinctive, nine-story German Renaissance-style structure — with its detailed stonework, reliefs, balconies, and gables — greatly helped to transform the neighborhood. It was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1976.

beats.script_body: The Dakota is famous for its roster of past and present celebrity residents, among them Judy Garland and Leonard Bernstein. Renamed "The Bramford," it was the film home of Rosemary and John Woodhouse — played by Mia Farrow and John Cassavetes — in the 1968 horror classic Rosemary's Baby. Yet it is almost impossible to step inside one of the Dakota's luxurious apartments: the residents are fiercely protective of their privacy, and a taciturn doorman guards the entrance at all hours.

beats.script_body: From handmade quilts and weathervanes to cookie jars and hunting decoys, this museum collects and displays folk art of the 18th and 19th centuries. While American art remains the main focus, it has expanded to include European and Latin American pieces, along with works by self-taught contemporary artists such as Henry Darger. The museum recently moved from its site alongside MoMA to the space opposite Lincoln Center, where it has staged exhibitions since 1989.

beats.script_body: Created by Frederick Law Olmsted, co-designer of Central Park, Riverside Park is much prized by local residents for its tranquility and superb facilities. Begin exploring at 70th Street, where you can also rent bicycles; Pier 1 at 70th Street is an ideal spot for fishing and relaxing, and a summer venue for free concerts and kids' shows. At the 79th Street Boat Basin you can glimpse yachts and sailboats or grab a snack at the Boat Basin Café. Of the park's 15 playgrounds, the River Run Playground at 82nd Street, with its miniature Hudson River, is one of the best. From 83rd Street, the half-mile Serpentine Promenade — a bike and running path — snakes past the Soldiers' and Sailors' Memorial to New Yorkers who died in the Civil War and the 91st Street Garden, its flowerbeds tended by die-hard volunteers.

A group of traditional masks made of wood and bark from Papua New Guinea ranks among its highlights.

A Discovery Room provides kids with hands-on activities, and the renovated IMAX theater shows movies every hour.

beats.script_body: No residential building in New York City is more iconic than the aptly named brownstone — long rows of these narrow, three-to-six-story homes distinguish neighborhoods on the Upper West Side and beyond. In New York, the term "brownstone" refers to any kind of row house, whether of brick, limestone, or marble. Beginning in the 1850s, brownstone quarried in Connecticut and New Jersey became the building material of choice, and everyone from middle-class families to the city's elite aspired to live in one — including the railroad magnate William H. Vanderbilt, who owned a $2 million pair at 640 and 642 Fifth Avenue.

beats.script_body: While much of the city had filled with densely packed brownstones by the late 1870s, the Upper West Side remained largely undeveloped until an elevated train arrived in 1879 and kicked off a period of huge growth. The architectural styles of that era — Queen Anne, Romanesque, and Renaissance Revival — encouraged unusual artistic freedom and eclecticism. On the Upper West Side, the houses were visually distinct from one another, often with different colored bricks and stone on a single facade, much to the taste of their socially competitive residents.
